steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Defined Vocabulary List (DVL) contains the words that may appear in GCSE Latin translation exams — approximately 400-500 words depending on the board.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Learning Latin vocabulary through English derivatives is highly effective: e.g. ambulare (to walk) → ambulance; videre (to see) → video; scribere (to write) → scribe/script.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Common Latin prefixes: trans- (across → transport), sub- (under → submarine), pre- (before → predict), re- (back/again → return), ex/e- (out of → export).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Common Latin suffixes: -tion (action/state from verb stems → narration from narro), -al (pertaining to → naval from navis), -ous (full of → furious from furia).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the Defined Vocabulary List and why is it important? | Q: Give three English derivatives from Latin verbs and their meanings. | Q: What English derivatives come from aqua, luna, and terra?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: The DVL is the official list of Latin words that may appear in the GCSE translation papers. Words outside the DVL are glossed in exams. It contains approximately 400-500 words that must be memorised. | Videre (to see) → video; scribere (to write) → scribble, scribe, script; audire (to hear) → audible, audience; dicere (to say) → dictate, diction; facere (to make/do) → factory, fact (any three). | Aqua (water) → aquatic, aqueduct, aquarium. Luna (moon) → lunar, lunatic. Terra (earth) → terrestrial, territory, terrain.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Systematically learn the DVL — use flashcards or spaced repetition, and test yourself on both Latin-to-English and English-to-Latin. When you encounter an unfamiliar word in the exam, check for a recognisable root or derivative to work out the meaning. Learn vocabulary in context: practise with whole sentences, not just isolated word lists. Pay attention to words that look similar but have different meanings (e.g. dare = to give, not 'to dare'; ferre = to carry, not 'to fear').
